claim: A velocity-level discrete Pressure Field Contact approximation preserves area-dependent net wrench behavior at useful computational cost, but it has no deformation or material-memory state and cannot represent buckling, folding, or general soft-body dynamics.
problem_and_setting: Efficient discrete-time simulation of distributed hydroelastic contact for rigid-body robotics using velocity-level time steppers while retaining finite-area force and moment effects.
method_or_mechanism: Each polygonal face becomes a compliant point constraint based on pressure rate and normal relative velocity; an implicit time update integrates it with velocity-level solvers. Polygonal surfaces reduce constraint count, but no volumetric deformation or history state is retained.
content_summary: Coin slide-spin stays within 1.3% of the analytical terminal ratio and shows first-order timestep and second-order moment-grid convergence. In a JACO pancake-flip task, polygonal tessellation uses 4.05 times fewer faces and solves 4.09 times faster, succeeding at all tested grids; physical controller transfer is author-reported. Tested geometry cost is linear and solver exponent about 1.3 over 230-1500 constraints. Area-dependent torque enables controlled spatula slip. Limits include linear tetrahedra, approximate moment integration, no deformation state, no buckling/folding, and thin/deep-contact equilibrium failures.
synthesis_role: Runtime and finite-area-wrench baseline for PFC, plus direct negative evidence against treating hydroelastic PFC as a stateful soft-tissue constitutive model.
development_link: Real-time PFC is not novel by itself. Add only minimal identifiable relaxation, hysteresis, heterogeneity, or evolving-contact state that changes decisions, and benchmark compute and failure regimes against this stateless baseline.

evidence.finding: Polygonal faces become compliant velocity-level constraints derived from pressure rate and normal relative velocity.
The solver is 0.01-0.5% from its discrete reference and within 1.3% of the analytical result, with first-order timestep and second-order moment-grid convergence.
Polygonal tessellation averages 4.05 times fewer faces and 4.09 times faster solution, with task success at all tested grids and author-reported hardware transfer.
Geometry cost is linear in faces and solver best-fit exponent about 1.3 for the tested 230-1500 constraint workload.
Distributed contact resolves area-dependent torque supporting controlled secure and loose grasp modes.
Implementation is limited to linear tetrahedra; moments are approximate; there is no deformation state; buckling/folding and some thin/deep contacts cannot be represented.

assumptions: One face constraint represents local contact
Pressure rate and velocity are sufficient
Finite-area wrench is the relevant detail

inferred: Pressure-rate updating is not viscoelastic memory
Pancake transfer does not validate tissue
Efficient PFC is not a novel impedance contribution
Added material state must justify compute and identification cost

conflicts_with: PFC as bulk deformation or material memory
Point contact captures all area-dependent torque
Claims about tissue validity, optimal impedance, passivity, or clinical safety

problem_lead_search_contexts.lead_statement: The valuable question is to identify the minimal contact representation that changes and improves optimal impedance decisions in continuous soft sliding, rather than presupposing that an HC-pressure-field hybrid is the correct method.
problem_lead_search_contexts.purpose: Compare pressure-field, elastic-foundation, and other finite-area contact representations against the proposed HC-consistent distributed model, emphasizing which measured wrench components and geometries are actually needed rather than assuming a more complex model is better.
problem_lead_search_contexts.expected_close_condition: Define the minimum contact representation and negative controls needed to distinguish scalar HC, distributed foundation, pressure-field, and unnecessary high-fidelity alternatives in the target task.
